body: Malaysian licence plates are black and generally have two white sections. This helps distinguish them from Indonesian plates, which have three sections.
Malaysia is the only Southeast Asian country to frequently use double white centre lines on its two-lane roads.
These thick yellow bars on the road are almost exclusive to Malaysia. Similar patterns are very rarely seen in Hong Kong and the United Kingdom.
Electricity poles in Malaysia often have black or white stickers. Sometimes you will also find red-and-white or red-and-blue stripes below the black sticker.
BERHENTI stop signs and BERI LALUAN yield signs are both unique to Malaysia.
Malaysian bollards will often have the colours black, white, grey and red. The layout is mostly the same across different varieties.
A typical Malaysian directional sign features hexagonal yellow highway shields, which are unique to Malaysia.
Malaysian kilometre markers have a unique white-and-blue colour scheme and often show the hexagon shields.
The Malay language uses the Latin script and is very closely related to Indonesian, making them practically indistinguishable to non-speakers.
In contrast to neighbouring Indonesia, Chinese characters are often seen in Malaysia, as 24.6% of the population is of Chinese descent.
Signposts in Malaysia almost always have black-and-white stripes. However, these are also found in Sri Lanka, Bhutan and Bangladesh, so check for other clues.
Black-and-white curbs are commonly found in Malaysia, but many other countries in Asia can also have them.
Each Malaysian state has its own road numbering system with a unique letter at the start of the road number.
Black pole stickers are most commonly found on the mainland. On Borneo, they only exist in Generation 4 coverage.
Black stickers with the text ‘TEL TNB’ at the bottom are only found in Johor.
White pole stickers are only found on electricity poles in Sarawak, on the island of Borneo.
Lamp posts with two small circles on the support are mainly found on mainland Malaysia.
Lamp posts with a triangular metal support are mainly found on mainland Malaysia.
Electricity poles in Sarawak typically have a 2-1 insulator configuration and a long diagonal wooden support. This is exclusive to the Sarawak region of Borneo.
Thin metal poles with two parallel pole tops are exclusive to the Sabah region of Borneo.
This lamp post with a supporting piece of sheet metal resembling a boomerang is found in Sarawak. It is more common in cities other than Kuching.
Trash bins with a logo resembling an ‘S’ are found in the states of Negeri Sembilan, Malacca and Johor.
Trash bins with a logo resembling leaves are found in Perlis and Kedah.
Trash bins with a logo featuring a sunny landscape and saying ‘Alam Flora’ are found in Pahang, Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya.
Yellow street name signs are specific to the state of Johor. This arrow-shaped street sign, regardless of its colour, is exclusive to Malaysia.
Green street signs that form an arrow shape and have a yellow hexagonal symbol with the letters JKR on the left side are found in Sabah.
On Borneo, the state of Sabah is very mountainous. In contrast, Sarawak generally has flatter roads with distant mountains.
Isolated rock formations, rising abruptly from an otherwise flat landscape, can be found near the Thai border in Perlis state.
Urban areas in Labuan are dotted with blue cylindrical containers.
This unique grey car with a long front antenna can be found in Gunung Mulu National Park, Sarawak.
